resources.string: Clear small tasks before they accumulate.
If something takes less than two minutes, do it now. Small tasks are cheap to finish and expensive to keep remembering.
Work in 25-minute sprints with real breaks.
A timer turns “work on it” into a small unit you can finish. Short breaks keep attention fresh across the day.
Sort tasks by importance, not by noise.
Urgent things shout; important things rarely do. Sorting both ways shows what deserves your best hours.
Count 5-4-3-2-1 and move before doubt starts.
Hesitation grows with every second. Counting down gives your brain a clear start signal before excuses arrive.
Attach a new habit to one you already have.
An existing habit is a reliable trigger. Tying a tiny new action to it removes the need to remember.
Explain it simply to find what you don’t know.
Explaining in plain words shows exactly where your understanding has gaps.
Decide what you’re deliberately not doing now.
Choosing what you won’t do protects your focus for the few goals that matter most.
Long, protected blocks for hard problems.
Hard problems need long, unbroken attention. Protecting it on purpose is a skill you can train.
Find the few actions that drive most of the result.
A small share of actions usually drives most of the result. Finding them first saves hours.
Return to what you learned at growing intervals.
Memory fades fast, but each well-timed recall makes it last longer.
Choose what you consume on purpose.
What you consume shapes what you think about. Choosing inputs on purpose frees attention.
Imagine the failure first, then prevent it.
Imagining failure in advance makes risks concrete while there’s still time to act.
Improve one small thing, every day.
Tiny improvements are easy to repeat, and they add up over weeks.
Three short questions to close the day.
A short look back turns a day of experience into a lesson for tomorrow.
